Crystal field splittings and magnetic ground state of the square-lattice antiferromagnets YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} with Jeff=1/2J_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/2

Abstract

We report on the crystal field level splitting and magnetic ground state of the Jeff=1/2J_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/2 square lattice antiferromagnets YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} using powder inelastic neutron scattering (INS) and neutron diffraction measurements. Both compounds exhibit a well-isolated Γ7\Gamma_{7} doublet ground state under a tetragonal crystal field environment, confirming a robust Jeff=1/2J_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/2 picture with slight XY-type anisotropic character in the gg-tensor. Notably, the ground state wave functions closely resemble the Γ7\Gamma_{7} doublet expected in the perfect cubic limit, consistent with the nearly cubic ligand configuration of eight O2 – \text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{}}\text{2\hskip 0.90417pt--\hskip 0.90417pt}} ions surrounding Yb3+. Below TNT_{\mathrm{N}} = 0.21 K, YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} exhibits a stripe long-range magnetic order characterized by an ordering wave vector 𝐪m\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{m}} = (1/2, 0, 0) or its symmetry-equivalent (0, 1/2, 0), with magnetic moments aligned along 𝐪m\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{m}}. The ordered moment is approximately 79% of the classical prediction, significantly larger than expected from the isotropic J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model, suggesting the possible involvement of exchange anisotropy in explaining this observation. We show that symmetry-allowed XXZ and bond-dependent anisotropic exchange terms in a square lattice can play a critical role in stabilizing the stripe order and suppressing the moment reduction as observed. These findings establish YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} as unique platforms for exploring rich Jeff=1/2J_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/2 magnetism from two less investigated perspectives: (i) on a square lattice and (ii) within a (nearly) cubic ligand environment.

I Introduction

The S=1/2S=1/2 square lattice antiferromagnet (SqAF) serves as a textbook model in the study of low-dimensional quantum magnetism [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. The Heisenberg model with isotropic nearest-neighbor (NN) and second NN antiferromagnetic interactions (the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} model) has been extensively studied for its potential to manifest a quantum spin liquid state (QSL) [6, 7, 8, 9]. The ratio J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} indicates the degree of additional quantum fluctuations induced by exchange frustration, which are maximized at J2=0.5​J1J_{2}=0.5J_{1}. Theoretical studies have shown that a QSL can emerge in the range 0.4<J2/J1<0.60.4<J_{2}/J_{1}<0.6, separating regions of two well-known magnetic orders: Néel-type (J2/J1<0.4J_{2}/J_{1}<0.4) and stripe-type (J2/J1>0.6J_{2}/J_{1}>0.6) [6, 7, 8, 9]. Notably, this phase diagram is very similar to that of the J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} Heisenberg model for S=1/2S=1/2 triangular lattice systems [10, 11, 12].

A compelling extension to these isotropic quantum spin models is exploring the effect of exchange anisotropy on quantum fluctuations. Such anisotropies can involve Ising- or planar-type XXZ anisotropies [13, 14, 15, 16], and more intriguingly, symmetry-allowed bond-dependent anisotropy terms [17, 18, 19, 20, 21], each of which capable of introducing unique magnetic properties. A key factor in the recent success of investigations on exchange anisotropy is the effective spin-1/2 degree of freedom in isolated Kramers doublet ground states (Jeff=1/2J_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/2), where the intrinsic coupling between spin and orbital degrees of freedom enables significant exchange anisotropy [22]. However, experimental studies of Jeff=1/2J_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/2 square lattice materials with exchange anisotropy have remained lacking, limiting insights into the anisotropic spin model in S=1/2S=1/2 SqAFs.

YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} have recently been suggested as nearly ideal realizations of a 2D Jeff=1/2J_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/2 square lattice antiferromagnet [23, 24]. These compounds crystallize in a tetragonal structure (PP4/m​m​mmmm space group), with Yb3+ ions forming layered square lattices [Fig. 1(a)] [25, 23]. Each Yb3+ ion is surrounded by a nearly cubic configuration of oxygen ligands with a marginal tetragonal distortion [da​b/dc=0.996d_{ab}/d_{c}=0.996, see Fig. 1(b)] [23]. The Jeff=1/2J_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/2 nature of the Yb3+ ions was inferred from heat capacity measurements, which revealed a total magnetic entropy of R​ln⁡(2)R\ln(2) [23, 24]. Temperature-dependent magnetic susceptibility [χ⁡(T)\chi(T)] of both compounds exhibits a broad maximum at a temperature TmaxT_{\mathrm{max}} = 0.33 K (0.38 K) in YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} (YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}), indicating the quasi-2D nature of their magnetic Hamiltonian [23]. While Ref. [23] reported the onset of 3D long-range order below TNT_{N} = 0.21 K (0.25 K) in YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} (YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}) based on a sharp lambda-like feature in C⁡(T)C(T), Ref. [24] presented a qualitatively different C⁡(T)C(T) curve and suggested the absence of long-range order. Most importantly, the presence of a sizable J2J_{2} was inferred from the much larger Curie-Weiss temperature magnitude (|θCW||\theta_{\mathrm{CW}}|) compared to TmaxT_{\mathrm{max}}, i.e., magnetic frustration, [23]. A quantitative estimation of J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} using high-temperature series expansion analysis of the isotropic J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} model, assuming J1>J2J_{1}>J_{2}, resulted in J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} close to 0.27 in these two compounds [23], within the Neél ordered phase.

These bulk properties strongly motivate further investigation into the microscopic magnetism of YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}, particularly regarding their spin Hamiltonians and associated quantum fluctuations. Notably, the simple theoretical analysis described above assumes an isotropic spin model, whereas the possibility of anisotropic exchange interactions between NNs should also be considered as potentially important in Jeff=1/2J_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/2 systems with edge-sharing ligand environments. Interestingly, YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} feature a cubic-like configuration of O2- ligands, entirely different from the octahedral ligand configurations that have been extensively studied [22, 26, 17, 19, 27, 28, 29]. This unique environment provides an opportunity to explore Jeff=1/2J_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/2 magnetism under entirely different conditions, potentially offering new insights into spin-orbital coupled interactions.

In this article, we present inelastic neutron scattering (INS) and neutron diffraction measurements of YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}, which reveal the crystal field splittings of Yb3+ ions and the long-range order of the Jeff=1/2J_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/2 magnetic moments in YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}. The crystal field levels measured by INS confirm that Yb3+ exhibits a Kramers doublet ground state separated by about 80 meV from the first excited states in both YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}, supporting the picture of Jeff=1/2J_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/2 square-lattice magnetism at the magnetic energy scale (∼\sim1 K). The crystal field Hamiltonian and the corresponding ground state wave function were derived by fitting the energy and dynamical structure factors of the measured excitations. This reveals a Γ7\Gamma_{7} doublet ground state not far from the perfect cubic limit but exhibits slight XY-type anisotropy in their gg-tensor. Powder neutron diffraction measurements of YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} at dilution refrigerator temperatures reveal magnetic Bragg peaks corresponding to an ordering wave vector 𝐪m\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{m}} = (1/2, 0, 0) or its symmetry-equivalent directions, indicating a stripe magnetic order, antithetical to the proposed order based upon high temperature susceptibility measurements. Rietveld refinement shows that the magnetic moments point along 𝐪m\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{m}}, with a magnitude 79% of the classical prediction without quantum fluctuations. We discuss a spin model and corresponding degree of quantum fluctuations for YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} compatible with these findings, suggesting that these compounds may host sizable exchange anisotropy beyond the isotropic J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model.

II Experimental details

Polycrystalline YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} were prepared by solid-state reaction as described in Ref. [23]. LuBi2​ClO4\text{LuBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and LuBi2​IO4\text{LuBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}, the nonmagnetic analogs of YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}, were synthesized by similar methods using reactions at 950∘C for 100 h followed by grinding and an additional heating step at 900∘C for 100 h. The Lu-based compounds are used in the INS measurements to quantify the extent of the signal due to phonon scattering.

INS measurements of the crystal field splitting were performed with the ARCS spectrometer at the Spallation Neutron Source at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL). Samples were loaded in aluminum (Al) sample cans with 1 atmosphere of helium gas. Data were collected using an incident energy of Ei=E_{i}= 160 meV, with the Fermi chopper set to 600 Hz, providing an energy resolution of =6.1=6.1 meV (full-width at half-maximum) at the elastic line. Background signals were estimated by measurements of nonmagnetic analogs LuBi2​ClO4\text{LuBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and LuBi2​IO4\text{LuBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} under the same temperature, using identical Al sample cans. Empty can measurements were subtracted from all datasets unless otherwise noted. Data processing was carried out using the Dave [31] and Mantid [32] software packages.

Powder neutron diffraction measurements of YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} were conducted with the HB-2A powder diffractometer at the High Flux Isotope Reactor at ORNL. To access temperatures below TNT_{\mathrm{N}} = 0.21 K, we used a dilution refrigerator. Approximately 9 g of polycrystalline YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} were loaded into a standard copper sample can. The can was filled with over-pressurized helium gas (p=10p=10 atm), which was necessary to ensure the sample fully thermalized at temperatures below TNT_{\mathrm{N}}. Data were collected using a wavelength of 2.41 Å at temperatures of 0.04 K, 0.25 K, and 1.5 K, with a counting time of approximately 8 hours per temperature. We used the FullProf software package to perform Rietveld refinement of crystal and magnetic structures [33].

III Results

III.1 Crystal field level splitting

Yb3+, a Kramers ion, has a J=7/2J=7/2 multiplet ground state (F7/22{}^{2}\mathrm{F}_{7/2} in term symbol formalism) that can split into a maximum of four Kramers doublets. In YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}, Yb3+ ions lie in a tetragonal environment coordinated by eight oxygen ions and two I or Cl ions [Fig. 1(b)], with the 4/m​m​m4/mmm site symmetry. This configuration results in four Kramers doublets and therefore should have three excited levels.

Our powder INS measurements successfully identified these three excited crystal field levels in YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}. Figures 2(a)–(b) show the powder INS spectra of YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} at 10 K with an incident neutron energy of 160 meV. Three clear, flat excitations are observed in both compounds as indicated by red arrows in Figs. 2(a)–(b). They exhibit higher intensity in the low-momentum (|𝐐||\mathbf{Q}|) region indicating the behavior of a magnetic form factor, and are absent in the INS spectra of the nonmagnetic analogs LuBi2​ClO4\text{LuBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and LuBi2​IO4\text{LuBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}. These observations confirm that the excitation signals correspond to Yb3+ crystal field levels.

Notably, all excited levels are located above 79 meV in both compounds, indicating that the ground-state Kramers doublet is well isolated at temperatures comparable to the magnetic energy scale (∼1\sim 1 K) of YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}. This ensures an exact Jeff=1/2J_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/2 picture, consistent with prior magnetic entropy measurements showing saturation at R​ln​(2)R\mathrm{ln}(2) [23]. In addition, no noticeable difference is observed between the spectra collected at 10 K and 100 K, as the activation energy (∼\sim80 meV) still dominates over the thermal fluctuation energy at 100 K.

The eigenvalues and relative dynamical structure factors of the three excited levels were analyzed quantitatively using constant wave-vector scans through the crystal field excitation spectra (integrated over the momentum range 4<|𝐐|<54<|\mathbf{Q}|<5\,Å-1), as shown in Figs. 3(a) and 3(e). These values were obtained by simultaneously fitting the three peaks with Lorentzian profiles, in which we refined the amplitude (= structure factors), center position (= eigenvalues), linewidth, and a global constant background. A multiplicative scaling factor was applied to the overall intensity during the fit.

The resultant eigenvalues and structure factor ratios, summarized in Table 1, provide crucial information of the tetragonal crystal field Hamiltonian and corresponding eigenstates of each compound. With the cc-axis as the unique tetragonal axis [see Fig. 1(b)], the crystal field Hamiltonian (ℋ^CF\mathcal{\hat{H}}_{\mathrm{CF}}) can be expressed as [34, 35]:

ℋ^CF\displaystyle\mathcal{\hat{H}}_{\mathrm{CF}} =\displaystyle= B20​𝒪^20+B40​𝒪^40+B44​𝒪^44+B60​𝒪^60+B64​𝒪^64,\displaystyle B_{2}^{0}\mathcal{\hat{O}}_{2}^{0}+B_{4}^{0}\mathcal{\hat{O}}_{4}^{0}+B_{4}^{4}\mathcal{\hat{O}}_{4}^{4}+B_{6}^{0}\mathcal{\hat{O}}_{6}^{0}+B_{6}^{4}\mathcal{\hat{O}}_{6}^{4}, (1)

where 𝒪^nm\mathcal{\hat{O}}_{n}^{m} are conventional Stevens operators [36], and BnmB_{n}^{m} are the corresponding crystal field parameters. This Hamiltonian yields the following four doublet states represented by two 2D irreducible representations, Γ7t\Gamma^{t}_{7} and Γ6t\Gamma^{t}_{6} [35]:

|Γ7,1t⟩\displaystyle\ket{\Gamma^{\mathrm{t}}_{7,1}} =±c1​|±52⟩±c2​|∓32⟩,\displaystyle=\pm c_{1}\ket{\pm\frac{5}{2}}\pm c_{2}\ket{\mp\frac{3}{2}},
|Γ7,2t⟩\displaystyle\ket{\Gamma^{\mathrm{t}}_{7,2}} =∓c1​|±52⟩±c2​|∓32⟩,\displaystyle=\mp c_{1}\ket{\pm\frac{5}{2}}\pm c_{2}\ket{\mp\frac{3}{2}},
|Γ6,1t⟩\displaystyle\ket{\Gamma^{\mathrm{t}}_{6,1}} =±a1​|∓72⟩±a2​|±12⟩,\displaystyle=\pm a_{1}\ket{\mp\frac{7}{2}}\pm a_{2}\ket{\pm\frac{1}{2}},
|Γ6,2t⟩\displaystyle\ket{\Gamma^{\mathrm{t}}_{6,2}} =∓a1​|∓72⟩±a2​|±12⟩,\displaystyle=\mp a_{1}\ket{\mp\frac{7}{2}}\pm a_{2}\ket{\pm\frac{1}{2}}, (2)

where MJM_{J} in |MJ⟩≡|J=7/2,MJ⟩\ket{M_{J}}\equiv\ket{J=7/2,M_{J}} denotes the eigenvalue of Jz^\hat{J_{z}}, and the normalized coefficients c1,2c_{1,2} and a1,2a_{1,2} depend on BnmB_{n}^{m}.

While determining BnmB_{n}^{m} is typically achieved by minimizing the χ2\chi^{2} metric between the observed and calculated crystal field spectra, this approach could potentially end up with multiple possible solutions. To ensure physically meaningful results based on sufficient constraints, we simultaneously fit the crystal field spectrum and the temperature-dependent magnetic susceptibility. This was performed by minimizing a custom-defined loss function using CrysFieldExplorer [37]:

Ltot\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{tot}} =\displaystyle= LSpectrum+L1/χ,\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{Spectrum}}+L_{\mathrm{1/\chi}}, (3)

where LSpectrumL_{\mathrm{Spectrum}} and L1/χL_{\mathrm{1/\chi}} are the loss functions concerning the crystal field spectra [Fig. 3(a) and 3(e)] and the inverse-susceptibility [Fig. 3(b) and  3(f)], respectively. LSpectrumL_{\mathrm{Spectrum}} is further defined as LE+LIntensityL_{E}+L_{\mathrm{Intensity}}. Their explicit functional expressions are:

LE=log10⁡(∑ind​e​t​{(Eexp​[i]+Ecal​[0])​I−HCF}2),\displaystyle L_{E}=\log_{10}\left(\sum_{i}^{n}det\{(E_{\mathrm{exp}}[i]+E_{\mathrm{cal}}[0])\mathrm{I}-H_{\mathrm{CF}}\}^{2}\right), (4)
LIntensity=∑in(Itrue​[i]−Icalc​[i])2(∑Itrue​[i])2,\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{Intensity}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{\sum_{i}^{n}({I_{\mathrm{true}}[i]-I_{\mathrm{calc}}}[i])^{2}}}{\sqrt{(\sum{I_{\mathrm{true}}}[i])^{2}}}, (5)
L1/χ=(1/χexp−1/χcalc)2(1/χexp)2.\displaystyle L_{1/\mathrm{\chi}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{({1/\mathrm{\chi}_{\mathrm{exp}}-1/\mathrm{\chi}_{\mathrm{calc}}})^{2}}}{\sqrt{({1/\mathrm{\chi}_{\mathrm{exp}}})^{2}}}. (6)

where the summation runs through 1 to nn-th crystal field levels of Yb3+. Eexp​[i]E_{\mathrm{exp}}[i] represents the energy levels of the observed crystal field excitations determined by fitting Lorentzian convolved Gaussians to the constant wave-vector scans in Figs. 3(a) and  3(e). Ecalc​[0]E_{\mathrm{calc}}[0] is eigenvalues obtained from the diagonalization of the crystal field Hamiltonian HCFH_{\mathrm{CF}} (Eq. (1)). I\mathrm{I} is the identity matrix. Itrue​[i]I_{\mathrm{true}}[i] and Icalc​[i]I_{\mathrm{calc}}[i] are the normalized observed and calculated intensities for the ii-th CEF excitation. χexp\mathrm{\chi}_{\mathrm{exp}} and χcalc\mathrm{\chi}_{\mathrm{calc}} denotes the experimentally measured and calculated magnetic susceptibility data. Details of the construction of the loss functions are demonstrated in Ref. [37].

The results of minimizing LtotL_{\mathrm{tot}} throughout the five-dimensional parameter space are shown in Fig. 3(c) and Fig. 3(g). The key term in Eq. (1) concerning the tetragonal nature of YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} is B20​𝒪^20B_{2}^{0}\mathcal{\hat{O}}_{2}^{0}. The other four terms are also allowed under cubic symmetry. Given the importance of B20B_{2}^{0}, we minimized LtotL_{\mathrm{tot}} for a fixed B20B_{2}^{0} value, repeating this process across a range of −2.5​meV<B20<1.5​meV-2.5\,\mathrm{meV}<B_{2}^{0}<1.5\,\mathrm{meV}.

For YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}, good fits were achieved by three solutions at B20=−1.48,−0.344,B_{2}^{0}=-1.48,-0.344, and 1.061.06 meV, as shown in Fig. 3(c) as a deep local minimum of the LtotL_{\mathrm{tot}} landscape. However, a careful analysis of their resultant ground states reveals that the cases of B20=−1.48B_{2}^{0}=-1.48 and 1.061.06\,meV exhibit unphysical features inconsistent with bulk characterization results, which is described in Appendix A. For YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}, we found two potential solutions at B20=−0.107B_{2}^{0}=-0.107 and 0.4870.487 meV [Fig. 3(g)], but further analysis could not conclusively distinguish between these solutions, as described below.

The full parameter set for each solution and the corresponding wave functions are summarized in TABLE. 2, along with their coefficients c1,2c_{1,2} and a1,2a_{1,2}. The uncertainty in the fitted BmnB^{n}_{m} values is estimated to be approximately 4 % of their magnitude, as such variations did not produce any noticeable visual disparity in our fit results (Fig. 3). Notably, except for B20B^{0}_{2}, the fitted BmnB^{n}_{m} values are very similar across all solutions, remaining nearly within the aforementioned uncertainty range. Indeed, the corresponding ground state doublet of each solution (Γ7,1t\Gamma^{t}_{7,1}) is close to each other, with coefficients c1c_{1} and c2c_{2} differing only slightly. This consistency aligns with previous findings that YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} show nearly the same magnetic properties [23]. The corresponding in-plane (ga​bg_{ab}) and out-of-plane (gcg_{c}) gg-factors of the ground state doublet, also listed in TABLE. 2, show a consistent profile across all solutions: ga​b>gcg_{ab}>g_{c}, confirming an XY-like anisotropic character of the single-ion Yb3+ magnetism in both YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}.

Another noteworthy observation is that the two excited doublets, |Γ6t⟩\ket{\Gamma^{t}_{6}}, are nearly pure |±12⟩\ket{\pm\frac{1}{2}} or |±72⟩\ket{\pm\frac{7}{2}} states, with minimal superposition between them. The key difference between the two solutions for YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} in TABLE. 2 lies in the energy hierarchy of |±12⟩\ket{\pm\frac{1}{2}} and |±72⟩\ket{\pm\frac{7}{2}}. Each solution assigns the observed excitations at ℏ​ω1\hbar\omega_{1} and ℏ​ω3\hbar\omega_{3} as either |12⟩\ket{\frac{1}{2}} and |72⟩\ket{\frac{7}{2}} or |72⟩\ket{\frac{7}{2}} and |12⟩\ket{\frac{1}{2}}. While the data at hand cannot resolve which assignment is correct, we emphasize that both solutions yield identical magnetic properties due to their quantitatively identical ground state wave functions. The first excited level–either |±12⟩\ket{\pm\frac{1}{2}} or |±72⟩\ket{\pm\frac{7}{2}}–is significantly separated from the ground state and would not affect the magnetic properties at temperatures comparable to the magnetic energy scale (∼1\sim 1 K).

Of further interest is the comparison between the observed M−HM-H curves in the paramagnetic regime (T≫|θCW|T\gg|\theta_{\mathrm{CW}}|) and the predictions from the fitted ground state doublet [Fig. 3(d) and 3(h)]. While the experimental curves are qualitatively consistent with theoretical expectations, showing saturation around 1.67​μB/Yb3+1.67\mu_{\mathrm{B}}/\mathrm{Yb}^{3+} (with an averaged gg-factor of (2​ga​b+gc)/3∼3.34(2g_{ab}+g_{c})/3\sim 3.34 for both compounds), we found apparent underestimation of magnetization values by the calculation in the high-field regime. The origin of this discrepancy remains unclear, but notably the deviation scales linearly with field strength.

Finally, it is useful to compare our results to the case of perfect cubic symmetry, characterized by the constraints B20=0B^{0}_{2}=0, B44=5​B40B^{4}_{4}=5B^{0}_{4}, and B64=−21​B60B^{4}_{6}=-21B^{0}_{6}. In the limit |B40|≫|B60||B^{0}_{4}|\gg|B^{0}_{6}| (see TABLE. 2), this symmetry yields the following Γ7\Gamma_{7} doublet ground state [38, 35]:

|Γ7c⟩\displaystyle\ket{\Gamma^{\mathrm{c}}_{7}} =32​|±52⟩−12​|∓32⟩.\displaystyle=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\ket{\pm\frac{5}{2}}-\frac{1}{2}\ket{\mp\frac{3}{2}}. (7)

This state is not far from the ground states found in YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}, with the fitted c1c_{1} and c2c_{2} coefficients showing a slight deviation from the cubic limit. Thus, despite the presence of the tetragonal characteristics, such as anisotropic gg-factors, to some extent YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} would retain the essence of Jeff=1/2J_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/2 magnetism typical of perfect cubic ligand environments. This aspect might be relevant to the nearly cubic arrangement of the eight oxygen anions surrounding Yb3+ [Fig. 1(b)], as evident in the near-unity ratio of in-plane to out-of-plane O–O distances (see TABLE 1) [23].

Thus, YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} offer a rare platform for studying Jeff=1/2J_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/2 magnetism in an edge-sharing (nearly) cubic environment. We note that, the magnitude of B20B^{0}_{2} in TABLE 2, which is the largest or second largest among the coefficients, should not be misinterpreted as it is the dominant term in the Hamiltonian. This is because, the contribution of higher order terms in Eq. 1 accompanies a few order-of-magnitude larger multiplication factor to BmnB^{n}_{m} in the solution and thus actually dominates over the lower order terms when their BmnB^{n}_{m} coefficients are comparable [35]. This becomes evident when examining the analytic form of, for instance, the phase factor ϕ7\phi_{7}, which is directly related to the wave function through c1=cos⁡(ϕ7/2)c_{1}=\cos{(\phi_{7}/2)} [35]:

tan⁡ϕ7=−23​(−15​B44+105​B64B20−50​B40−1470​B60).\displaystyle\tan{\phi_{7}}={-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\left(\frac{-15B^{4}_{4}+105B^{4}_{6}}{B^{0}_{2}-50B^{0}_{4}-1470B^{0}_{6}}\right)}. (8)

We note that the definition of BmnB^{n}_{m} used in this work [Eq. (1)] is different from that in Ref. [35] by constant multiplication factors.

III.2 Magnetic structure

The magnetic long-range order in YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} was investigated using powder neutron diffraction with a dilution refrigerator. The crystal structure of YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} has previously been studied via Rietveld refinement of time-of-flight neutron diffraction profiles collected at TT = 30 K [23]. We conducted the same analysis on new data collected at T=1.5​KT=1.5K, still far above TNT_{\mathrm{N}} [Fig. 4(a)]. The refinement result is nearly identical to that reported in our previous work [23], with no significant differences observed.

Neutron diffraction measurements at 40 mK, well below TNT_{\mathrm{N}}, revealed the emergence of magnetic Bragg peaks in YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} [Fig. 4(b)], demonstrating the onset of long-range order. This diffraction profile corresponds to a magnetic ordering wave vector 𝐪m\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{m}} = (1/2, 0, 0) (reciprocal lattice units, r.l.u.) or its symmetry-equivalent 𝐪m\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{m}} = (0, 1/2, 0). For clarity, we will describe our findings based on 𝐪m\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{m}} = (1/2, 0, 0) hereafter. This ordering wave vector generates an alternating configuration of ferromagnetic spin chains, typically referred to as a stripe [6] or columnar-type magnetic order [39]. Notably, in the isotropic S=1/2S=1/2 J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} model, such a magnetic structure is expected only for J2/J1>0.6J_{2}/J_{1}>0.6, which is significantly larger than the J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} ratio predicted for YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} from high-temperature series expansion analysis [23]. Additionally, the parallel alignment between 2D square-lattice layers implies the sign of interlayer interactions: assuming additional interlayer couplings are negligible, the NN interlayer interaction is inferred to be ferromagnetic.

The direction of magnetic moments was unambiguously determined by the absence of intensity at the (12\frac{1}{2}00) at 2​θ=18∘2\theta=18^{\circ} [Fig. 4(b)]. This indicates that magnetic moments are parallel to 𝐪m\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{m}} [i.e., along the a-axis for 𝐪m\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{m}} = (1/2, 0, 0)], as only this orientation suppresses the (12\frac{1}{2}00) peak by making its neutron polarization factor zero. This is evident in the comparison between our data to simulated diffraction patterns for the 𝐪m\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{m}} = (1/2, 0, 0) magnetic structure with moments along the aa, bb, and cc directions [black solid lines in Fig. 4(b)]. Also, the observed magnetic Bragg peak intensities are well described by the model with moments parallel to 𝐪m\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{m}} (the aa-axis). Finally, quantitative refinement of the peak intensities yields an ordered moment magnitude of 1.53(4)μB/Yb3+\mu_{\mathrm{B}}/\mathrm{Yb}^{3+} for YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}.

Fig. 5 shows the temperature dependence of the diffraction intensity at 2​θ=22.6∘2\theta=22.6^{\circ}, corresponding to the (12\frac{1}{2}01) peak. The data reveal the emergence of the magnetic Bragg peak below around 0.21 K. This is consistent with TNT_{\mathrm{N}} = 0.21 K for YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} obtained from heat capacity measurements [23], also shown in Fig. 5.

IV Discussion

The combination of crystal field splitting and the magnetic ground state presented in this work provides crucial insights concerning the nature of magnetism in YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}. The observed stripe magnetic order highlights the importance of exchange interactions beyond antiferromagnetic J1J_{1}, as the J1J_{1}-only model predicts a Neél-type order with 𝐪m\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{m}}=(1/2, 1/2, 0). Given the similarity in bulk properties [23] and ground state wave functions, we infer that YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} likely adopts the same 𝐪m\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{m}}=(1/2, 0, 0) ground state, although the moment direction could differ. The simplest interpretation for this observation is the presence of strong antiferromagnetic J2J_{2}: in the isotropic J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model, J2/J1>0.6J_{2}/J_{1}>0.6 stabilizes the stripe order [6, 7, 8, 9].

However, the isotropic S=1/2S=1/2 J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} model reveals limitations in describing other observations. Combining neutron diffraction (1.53(4)μB/Yb3+\mu_{\mathrm{B}}/\mathrm{Yb}^{3+}) with crystal field splitting analysis (ga​b=3.85g_{ab}=3.85), the observed ordered moment magnitude in YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} corresponds to the 79(2) % of the classical prediction. This 21 % reduction is much smaller than the 40 % reduction typically expected from the isotropic S=1/2S=1/2 J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} model (in the absence of significant exchange frustration, i.e., J2≫J1J_{2}\gg J_{1} or J1≫J2J_{1}\gg J_{2}), as confirmed by both experiment and theories [40, 41, 42, 6, 43]. Moreover, the reduction increases further as J2J_{2} and J1J_{1} become more comparable since it drives the model closer to the QSL region, 0.4<J2/J1<0.60.4<J_{2}/J_{1}<0.6. While interlayer coupling (JcJ_{c}) can remedy this discrepancy, a large separation between adjacent square lattice layers [Fig. 1(a)], a broad maximum in temperature-dependent magnetic susceptibility [23, 24], and preliminary estimations based on density functional theory electronic structure [24] consistently suggest its very weak strength. Thus, incorporating JcJ_{c}–likely only a few percent of J1J_{1} or J2J_{2}–may not suppress the moment reduction enough to the level observed [44, 42].

The above conclusion motivates us to explore the possibility of magnetic anisotropy in YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}. The symmetry-allowed interaction matrix between NN Yb3+ sites can be expressed as follows (using the parametrization notation of Δ\Delta and J±⁣±J_{\pm\pm} commonly applied in other lattice models [20, 45]):

ℋ^i​j=𝐒iT​(J1+2​J±⁣±​c~i​j000J1−2​J±⁣±​c~i​j000Δ​J1)​𝐒j,\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{H}}_{ij}=\mathbf{S}_{i}^{T}\begin{pmatrix}J_{1}+2J_{\pm\pm}\tilde{c}_{ij}&0&0\\ 0&J_{1}-2J_{\pm\pm}\tilde{c}_{ij}&0\\ 0&0&\Delta J_{1}\end{pmatrix}\mathbf{S}_{j}, (9)

where 𝐒i\mathbf{S}_{i} is the (effective) spin operator acting on the localized moment at site ii of a square lattice, c~i​j=cos⁡(2​ϕi​j)\tilde{c}_{ij}=\cos(2\phi_{ij}), with ϕi​j\phi_{ij} being the angle between the a-axis and the bond vector connecting sites ii and jj. In other words, c~i​j=±1\tilde{c}_{ij}=\pm 1 for the bonds along a- and b-directions, respectively.

The parameter Δ\Delta quantifies the degree of XXZ exchange anisotropy. The in-plane spin configuration found in YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} indicates that only the easy-plane type (Δ<1\Delta<1) is compatible. While reducing Δ\Delta from 1 does not significantly alter the phase boundaries between Neél-type and stripe magnetic orders in the isotropic J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model, it gradually suppresses quantum fluctuations inherent to the isotropic model [43]. Notably, this behavior is very similar to the role of Δ<1\Delta<1 in S=1/2S=1/2 triangular lattice systems [16, 13, 20]. Calculations in Ref. [43] suggest that achieving a moment reduction as small as 20 % roughly requires Δ<0.7\Delta<0.7, a significant level of easy-plane anisotropy. Thus, strong easy-plane XXZ anisotropy could be one possibility of the suppressed moment reduction.

Another component, J±⁣±J_{\pm\pm}, represents bond-dependent exchange anisotropy. Notably, J±⁣±=±0.5​J1J_{\pm\pm}=\pm 0.5J_{1} corresponds to the pure quantum compass model [46]. The classical phase diagram of the J1−J2−J±⁣±J_{1}-J_{2}-J_{\pm\pm} model provides qualitative insights into the influence of J±⁣±J_{\pm\pm} on the competition between Neél-type and stripe long-range orders (Fig. 6). Interestingly, J±⁣±J_{\pm\pm} favors the observed stripe order over the Néel order, regardless of its sign, significantly expanding the stripe phase compared to the isotropic J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model. We found that J±⁣±>0J_{\pm\pm}>0 produces a stripe configuration consistent with our observations, where the magnetic moments align parallel to 𝐪m\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{m}} (Fig. 6). This makes our findings in YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} compatible with either a large J2/J1>0J_{2}/J_{1}>0, a large J±⁣±/J1>0J_{\pm\pm}/J_{1}>0, or a combination of both.

More importantly, increasing |J±⁣±||J_{\pm\pm}| is expected to gradually suppress the moment reduction in the stripe phase. In this phase, J±⁣±J_{\pm\pm} induces an energy gap in the Goldstone mode at 𝐐=𝐪m\mathbf{Q}=\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{m}}, reducing zero-point fluctuations and thereby suppressing the moment reduction. A quantitative estimation of this effect requires advanced quantum-mechanical simulations of the J1−J2−J±⁣±J_{1}-J_{2}-J_{\pm\pm} model. Such simulations are particularly valuable for examining how the known range of the QSL phase in the isotropic model (0.4<J2/J1<0.60.4<J_{2}/J_{1}<0.6) evolves under finite J±⁣±J_{\pm\pm}.

Given the compatibility of our observations with the two symmetry-allowed anisotropies, assessing their feasibility from a microscopic structural perspective is a crucial direction for further investigation. Numerous studies have shown that Jeff=1/2J_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/2 moments in edge-shared octahedral ligand configurations can exhibit substantial anisotropic exchange interactions, in both transition metal and rare-earth based systems [22, 26, 17, 19, 27, 28, 29]. Since YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} also feature Jeff=1/2J_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/2 moments in an edge-shared ligand environment, there is no a priori reason to exclude the possibility of such interactions. However, the interaction profiles strongly depend on the specific orbital arrangements of the magnetic ions and ligands. Unfortunately, theoretical studies on the cubic ligand network is still lacking. In Appendix B, we note both the important similarities and differences between octahedral and cubic ligand configurations, highlighting the challenges in drawing intuitive conclusions for cubic environments.

Experimental insights into Jeff=1/2J_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/2 magnetism in cubic ligand environments are also limited due to the scarcity of relevant materials other than YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}. A comparable material class is the Yb-based pyrochlore oxides YbM22{}_{2}M_{2}O7 (MM = Ti, Ge, Sn), where Yb3+ is surrounded by an edge-shared polyhedron of eight oxygens [47]. Notably, INS studies on these materials revealed significant exchange anisotropy [48, 49, 50]. That being said, their oxygen configurations are substantially distorted from the ideal cubic form, limiting the direct applicability of these findings to YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}.

Overall, our experimental results suggest the potential presence of exchange anisotropy in YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} (and possibly YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}). Determining the generalized spin Hamiltonian of these systems using cold-neutron spectroscopy is essential to unambiguously confirm this possibility. Regardless, our findings suggest that YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} open a new avenue for exploring the rich Jeff=1/2J_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/2 magnetism from two perspectives: (i) on a square lattice (ii) within a nearly cubic ligand environment–both of which have been far less studied compared to the extensively investigated triangular or honeycomb systems with octahedron environments.

V Conclusion

We have studied the crystal field level splitting and magnetic ground state of the Jeff=1/2J_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/2 square lattice antiferromagnets YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}. Under the tetragonal crystal field environment, both compounds exhibit a well-isolated Γ7t\Gamma^{t}_{7} doublet ground state, confirming a robust Jeff=1/2J_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/2 picture with a slight XY-type anisotropic g-tensor (ga​b/gcg_{ab}/g_{c} = 1.42 and 1.73 in YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}, respectively). The refined ground state wave functions in both compounds resemble the Γ7c\Gamma^{c}_{7} doublet expected in the perfect cubic limit, which might be attributed to marginal tetragonal distortion [23] in the nearly cubic ligand configuration of eight O2- ions. YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} exhibits a stripe long-range order below TNT_{\mathrm{N}} = 0.21 K, indicating the presence of interactions beyond the isotropic J1J_{1}. The refined ordered moment is ∼\sim79 % of its classical prediction, considerably larger than that predicted by the isotropic S=1/2S=1/2 J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model (∼\sim60 %), which would not be fully attributed to interlayer coupling. Interestingly, symmetry-allowed XXZ and bond-dependent anisotropy terms both favor the observed magnetic structure and the suppressed moment reduction. Further investigations, including theoretical estimations of the exchange interaction profile and experimental studies using cold-neutron spectroscopy, are essential to validate the suggested anisotropic spin Hamiltonian. Our findings suggest that YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} provide a rare opportunity to explore rich Jeff=1/2J_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/2 magnetism (i) on a square lattice and (ii) within a nearly cubic ligand environment.

Appendix B Comparing octahedral and cubic ligand configurations

Here, we highlight some crucial similarities and differences between Jeff=1/2J_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/2 magnetism in the widely studied traditional octahedral ligand configuration and our case with a nearly cubic environment [27]. First, the doublet ground state found in YbBi2​IO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} and YbBi2​ClO4\text{YbBi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ClO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}} (Table. 2), which is not far from the perfect cubic case [Eq. (7)], falls into the same Γ7\Gamma_{7} representation as the Jeff=1/2J_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/2 doublet realized in transition metal systems with octahedral ligand configurations (e.g., d5d^{5} iridates and ruthenates, and d7d^{7} cobaltates) [27, 28]. It is also noteworthy that 4f1f^{1} rare-earth systems with the octahedral environment (e.g., Ce3+), which were suggested to exhibit strong antiferromagnetic Kitaev interactions, also configures the same Γ7\Gamma_{7} ground state doublet as Γ7t\Gamma^{t}_{7} in Eq. () [28]. Second, concerning the NN superexchange interactions, both configurations consist of two symmetry-equivalent exchange paths [see Fig. 1(b)]. On the other hand, a contrasting feature is the bond angle: unlike a 90∘ bond angle found in the octahedral configuration, the cubic configuration is characterized by a tetrahedral bond angle, cos−1(−1/3)=109.47∘\mathrm{cos}^{-1}({-1/3})=109.47^{\circ}. Each aspect crucially influences the underlying hopping processes and the net exchange interaction matrix, thereby difficult to infer what would happen in the cubic case without explicit calculation of the hopping processes.
